title: Best AI Detectors for Teachers: 8 Tools Tested for Classroom Use
summary: I tested 8 AI detectors for teachers on ESL false positives, humanizer resilience, FERPA compliance, and cost. Pangram leads.
body_markdown:
88% of students used AI for assessments in 2025-26, up from 53% one year earlier. AI academic misconduct is up 400% since 2022. Yet when researcher Mike Perkins evaluated 14 AI-detection tools, not one scored above 80% accuracy.


So where does that leave you? Searching for the best AI detectors for teachers that actually work with real students, real budgets, and real consequences for getting it wrong.


I tested eight tools against five criteria: accuracy on humanized/edited content, ESL false positive rates, FERPA/COPPA compliance, cost-per-student, and LMS integration depth.


## Quick Verdict:


- **Best overall:** Pangram (99.98% accuracy, near-zero false positives, catches paraphrased AI)
- **Best free tier:** GPTZero (10,000 words/month, 380,000+ educators)
- **Best for ESL/multilingual classrooms:** Copyleaks (lowest ESL false positive rate at ~13%)
- **Best for process-based verification:** Grammarly Authorship (free on every tier, shows how the work was written)
- **Best for teacher teams:** Originality.ai (shared dashboards, audit trails, flexible pricing)


No AI detector should be sole proof of misconduct. These are conversation starters, not courtroom evidence.


## Key Takeaways


**No score is proof.** Every vendor warns against using detection alone, and courts have upheld students’ due process rights in misconduct cases


**Pangram is the most accurate tool tested.** 99.98% accuracy, near-zero false positives, and the only one that reliably catches paraphrased AI


**Most detectors miss humanizer output.** GPTZero drops to 18%, QuillBot to roughly 60% on hybrid text. 150+ humanizer tools now pull 33.9 million monthly visits


**ESL false positives vary wildly.** Pangram 0%, Copyleaks ~13%, Turnitin 18%, GPTZero 38%. A Stanford study found detectors flagged 61.3% of TOEFL essays by non-native speakers as AI-generated


**Free options exist.** GPTZero gives 10,000 words per month, QuillBot needs no signup, and Grammarly Authorship is free on every tier and shows how the work was written

## 1. Pangram: Best AI Detector for Teachers Overall


I recommend[Pangram](https://affiliate.pangram.com/b4m9mcquz0sa?wct-an=on) to everyone these days, not just teachers. If you need to detect possible AI content, but you don’t want to risk accusing everyone of being GPT-dependent without a good cause, Pangram is fantastic. It has the lowest false positive rate of any tool here, and it’s accuracy is still through the roof. Pangram even works better for detecting AI-assisted text or rewritten LLM content than anything else I’ve tried.


It’s also brilliant for the kind of work teachers do. It has plenty of LMS integrations with things like Google Classroom and Canvas, plus a Chrome extension. The Google Docs integration highlights sections exhibiting AI-writing or AI-assistance signals directly within the document workflow. It even supports bulk uploads and OCR on every plan, and it works in 20 languages.


ESL performance is actually incredible here. In Pangram’s evaluation using the same 91 TOEFL essays included in the Stanford detector-bias study, Pangram recorded zero false positives.


#### ✓ What we like about Pangram


- 99.98% accuracy rate and a false positive rate of almost zero
- Image detection now bundled into every plan at no extra cost
- Far better than most tools on paraphrased (or humanized) AI writing
- Insights into AI-assisted and AI-written text
- Integrates with Canvas, Google Classroom, Google Docs, and more
- Useful Chrome extension for online scanning
- Support for more than 20 languages
- Doesn’t train models on student or academic information
- Includes plagiarism detection on paid plans


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Pangram


- Four free scans a day won’t be enough for most teachers
- Paid plan is more expensive than some alternatives
- Can struggle with niche formats and very short snippets of text


### How Much Does Pangram Cost?


There is a free tier which gives you up to 2,000 words of text per day, but that won’t be enough for most teachers. The paid plans start at $20 per month for up to 300,000 words, which might be a good starting point. Larger institutions will probably end up choosing the $65 per month option though, which gives you up to 1.5 million words per month.


Both paid plans include plagiarism detection and social feed scanning, plus 100 image scans on the $20 tier and 500 on the $65 tier. Every plan gives you AI assistance detection, interpretability features, bulk file uploads, OCR scanning, support for more than 20 languages, the browser extension, plus the Google Docs integration. Also, you get the same level of accuracy on every plan.


#### Pangram is suitable for:


- Teachers reviewing academic work who don’t want to make false accusations
- Teachers who also need to check submitted images or diagrams
- ESL and multilingual classes (plus coding work)
- Schools using Canvas or Google Classrooms
- Educators who need to separate AI editing help from AI-generated work
- Teachers checking possible AI content in Google Docs


#### Pangram is not suitable for:


- Educators who need a big free plan
- One-sentence answers, or content with niche formatting
- Absolute evidence for academic misconduct


**Bottom line:** Pangram might be more expensive than some of the tools on this list, but I’d prefer to pay the extra and get results I can actually trust. It catches rewritten AI content better, gives teachers a better insight into how AI might have been used, and keeps false positive rates to a minimum.


## 2. GPTZero: Best Free AI Detector for Individual Teachers


If you’re a teacher looking for immediate AI detection without a purchase order, GPTZero is where you start. The free tier gives you 10,000 words per month, enough for a classroom’s worth of essays. More than 380,000 educators already use it, making it the most widely adopted teacher-facing detector on the market.


Paid plans run $10-16/month and unlock batch scanning plus the Writing Report feature, which shows revision history and writing patterns over time. Processing speed is the fastest I tested. Results come back in 8-18 seconds, compared to 30+ seconds for several competitors. That speed matters when you’re grading a stack of 30 essays on a Sunday night.


#### ✓ What we like about GPTZero


- Generous free tier (10,000 words/month)
- Fastest processing speed of any tool tested (8-18 seconds)
- Writing Report with revision history tracking
- Education-first design with 380,000+ teacher community
- Integrates with Canvas, Moodle, and Google Classroom


#### ✗ What we don’t like about GPTZero


- 38% ESL false positive rate
- Only 18% detection rate on humanized content
- Scan limits on free and lower-paid tiers
- One teacher uploaded their own PhD dissertation and GPTZero scored it 89-91% AI-generated


### How Much Does GPTZero Cost?


The free tier provides 10,000 words per month. Paid plans run $10-16/month and unlock batch scanning plus the Writing Report feature. At scale, the cost works out to about $1.27 per student. Shaker Heights City School District pays $5,600/year to cover 27 teachers and 4,400 students.


AFT President Randi Weingarten called GPTZero “a magnifying glass to help teachers get a closer look.” The education-first design shows in every screen. But that magnifying glass also reveals the flaws. GPTZero reports 99.3% overall accuracy, but that number masks serious gaps. The ESL false positive rate sits at 38%. For classrooms with non-native English speakers, that’s a devastating problem.


#### GPTZero is suitable for:


- Teachers who need immediate detection without a purchase order
- Educators with zero budget who need a reliable starting point
- Classrooms with primarily native English speakers


#### GPTZero is not suitable for:


- ESL or multilingual classrooms (38% false positive rate)
- Schools where students actively use humanizer tools (18% detection on humanized content)
- Sole evidence for academic misconduct


**Bottom line:** The best starting point if you have zero budget. Just don’t use it as sole evidence, especially with ESL students.


## 3. Turnitin: Best for Institutions Already Using It


If your school already pays for Turnitin, you have an AI detector built in. That single fact makes it the default choice for more than 30,000 institutions worldwide. The AI detection module sits right inside the same interface your teachers already know, with zero setup friction and no new training required.


For GPT-5 and Gemini output, Turnitin’s detection is excellent. I found 98-100% accuracy on standard AI-generated text over 300 words. The tool has processed 38+ million student essays since its AI detection launched in April 2023.


#### ✓ What we like about Turnitin


- Already installed at most institutions (30,000+ worldwide)
- Strong GPT-5 and Gemini detection (98-100%)
- Massive plagiarism database for combined checking
- Familiar interface requiring minimal teacher training


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Turnitin


- 53-60% accuracy on Claude-generated content
- 18% ESL false positive rate
- Institution-only purchasing, no individual access
- Most expensive per-student cost ($2.59-3.19/year)
- The Brittany Carr case: a Liberty University student wrote a personal essay about cancer and depression, Turnitin flagged it as AI-generated, and she left the university


### How Much Does Turnitin Cost?


Turnitin costs $2.59-3.19 per student per year, the most expensive on this list. Broward County’s three-year contract exceeds $550,000 for 230,000 students. Multiple districts across Utah, Ohio, and Alabama are spending similar amounts. Individual teachers can’t purchase it directly. You need institutional adoption, which means navigating bureaucracy and budget cycles.


The problem is Claude. Detection rates on Claude-generated content drop to 53-60%, and students are increasingly aware of which models are harder to detect. Even Turnitin’s own CPO, Annie Chechitelli, has acknowledged the false positive risk. At UC San Diego, student Aldan Creo put it bluntly: “If we write properly, we get accused of being AI.”


#### Turnitin is suitable for:


- Institutions that already have Turnitin contracts in place
- Schools where most student work exceeds 300 words
- Environments where teachers prefer a familiar, embedded interface


#### Turnitin is not suitable for:


- Individual teachers without institutional purchasing power
- Schools where students frequently use Claude
- ESL-heavy classrooms (18% false positive rate)
- Sole basis for academic misconduct charges


**Bottom line:** Use it if your school already has it. Don’t rely on it alone for Claude-generated content or ESL students. Pair it with GPTZero or Copyleaks for a second opinion.


## 4. Copyleaks: Best for ESL and Multilingual Classrooms


A Stanford study found that 61.22% of TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers were wrongly flagged as AI-generated. Chinese students faced a 61.3% false positive rate, compared to just 5.1% for US students. If you teach ESL or multilingual classes, those numbers should alarm you.


Copyleaks is the exception to the ESL accuracy problem. This detector reports 99.84% accuracy specifically on non-native English text, with an ESL false positive rate of roughly 13%. Compare that to GPTZero’s 38% and Turnitin’s 18%. Both the University of Michigan-Dearborn and SMU switched from Turnitin to Copyleaks precisely because of this difference.


#### ✓ What we like about Copyleaks


- Lowest ESL false positive rate of any tool tested (~13%)
- Supports 100+ languages natively
- Combined AI detection and plagiarism checking in a single scan
- Affordable at $10.99/month for individuals
- Chrome extension and Google Docs add-on for in-browser scanning


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Copyleaks


- Credit-based system limits monthly scans
- 85% accuracy on manually edited AI content
- Some false positive variance across document types


### How Much Does Copyleaks Cost?


Copyleaks costs $10.99/month for individual teachers. The credit-based system creates a ceiling: once you burn through your monthly credits, you’re either waiting or paying more.


The tool supports over 100 languages and combines AI detection with plagiarism checking in a single scan. Overall detection accuracy hits 99.6 out of 100. Soheil Feizi from the University of Maryland warns broadly that AI detectors “have a very high false-positive rate, and can be pretty easily evaded.” Copyleaks doesn’t solve evasion, but it does solve the false positive problem for the students most vulnerable to it.


#### Copyleaks is suitable for:


- Multilingual and ESL classrooms where false accusations carry outsized harm
- Teachers who need combined AI detection and plagiarism checking
- Schools with linguistically diverse student populations


#### Copyleaks is not suitable for:


- Teachers who need unlimited scanning without credit limits
- Schools primarily concerned about humanizer tool evasion


**Bottom line:** Best for multilingual and ESL classrooms where false accusations carry outsized harm. Skip if you need unlimited scanning without worrying about credits.


## 5. Grammarly Authorship: Best for Process-Based Verification


Every other tool on this list looks at a finished document and guesses. Grammarly Authorship watches the document get written and reports what actually happened. That is a different product category, and for a lot of teachers it is the more useful one.


Authorship labels text as typed by the student, generated by AI, pasted from a website, or edited with Grammarly. You get a circle graph showing the split, sentence-level color coding, and a full replay of the writing session from blank page to submission. That matters because of a number covered further down this page: combining detector output with revision history raises accuracy to roughly 75%, according to John Grady’s research. Authorship makes revision history a standard part of submission instead of something you go digging for after a bad score lands.


Scale is the other argument. Grammarly serves more than 40 million people across 3,000+ institutions, and Authorship runs in Google Docs, Microsoft Word, Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle. At one R1 university, 90% of students said the Authorship data was easy to understand. Adoption friction is close to zero because most of your students already have Grammarly installed.


#### ✓ What we like about Gramarly


- Free on every tier, including Grammarly’s free plan
- Shows how the work was written instead of a probability score students can argue with
- Full document replay, including where students got stuck
- Sentence-level attribution across typed, AI-generated, pasted, and Grammarly-edited text
- Works in Google Docs, Word, Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle
- Generates APA, MLA, and Chicago citations alongside the report
- 3,000+ institutions already on Grammarly for Education


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Grammarly Authorship


- Not retroactive. Students need Authorship active while writing, so it only works as a submission policy
- A student who retypes AI output by hand produces a clean report
- Pasted text gets flagged as pasted even when the source is the student’s own notes
- Requires setting expectations with students up front, which is more work than a copy-paste scan


### How Much Does Grammarly Authorship Cost?


Nothing. Authorship is included in Grammarly’s free plan as well as Pro, with no premium subscription required. Institutional Grammarly for Education licensing is quoted per school and adds admin controls and Data Processing Agreements, but an individual teacher can ask students to submit Authorship reports today at zero cost to anyone.


That pricing is exactly why it pairs with a paid detector rather than replacing one. Run Pangram or Copyleaks on the finished text and require an Authorship report alongside it. When the two disagree, you have a conversation to start instead of a number to defend.


#### Grammarly Authorship is suitable for:


- Teachers who want evidence of process, not a probability score
- Schools building AI policy around disclosure rather than surveillance
- Classrooms where students already use Grammarly
- Any teacher who has had a detection score challenged by a parent or administrator


#### Grammarly Authorship is not suitable for:


- Spot-checking work that has already been submitted
- Teachers who cannot set submission requirements in advance
- Catching AI in text written outside Grammarly-connected apps


**Bottom line:** The strongest complement to a detector on this list, and it costs nothing. It will not catch a student who plans around it, but it turns “prove you wrote this” from an accusation into a file the student hands you.


## 6. Winston AI: Best for Paper and Scanned Submissions


Most AI detectors require digital text. Copy-paste or file upload, nothing else. Winston AI breaks that pattern with built-in OCR that processes scanned documents and even handwritten submissions.


If your students still turn in paper assignments, or if you teach at a school where not every classroom is 1:1 with devices, that feature alone sets Winston apart. I found no other detector in this roundup that handles physical submissions natively.


#### ✓ What we like about Winston AI


- OCR for scanned and handwritten submissions
- 99% claimed accuracy on AI-generated text
- Plagiarism checking against 400 billion web pages
- Google Classroom integration with unlimited premium seats
- Downloadable PDF reports for academic integrity cases


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Winston AI


- Only 6 supported languages (vs. Copyleaks’ 100+)
- Less established K-12 track record than competitors
- Key features locked behind paid tier ($18/month)


### How Much Does Winston AI Cost?


Winston AI’s premium plan runs $18/month and includes batch processing and unlimited seats. A free trial with credits lets you test before committing.


Beyond OCR, the numbers hold up. Winston claims 99% accuracy on standard AI-generated text and runs plagiarism checks against 400 billion web pages. The platform generates downloadable PDF reports for each scan. Those reports create a paper trail for academic integrity cases, which administrators and parents tend to appreciate.


#### Winston AI is suitable for:


- Teachers whose students submit paper or handwritten assignments
- Schools without 1:1 device ratios
- Educators who need PDF documentation for integrity cases


#### Winston AI is not suitable for:


- Multilingual classrooms (only 6 languages)
- Budget-constrained teachers looking for free options


**Bottom line:** Winston AI is the only pick that handles paper submissions natively. If your classroom still runs on printed work, it fills a gap nothing else does.


## 7. Originality.ai: Best for Teacher Teams and Departments


When five or more teachers need shared AI detection, individual accounts become a management headache. Originality.ai was built for exactly this scenario. Team features include shared dashboards, audit trails, and centralized billing.


#### ✓ What we like about Originality.ai


- Team audit trails with timestamps and confidence scores
- Combined AI detection, plagiarism, and fact-checking suite
- Flexible pricing (subscription or pay-as-you-go)
- Chrome extension and API access for power users
- Shareable reports streamline multi-teacher review workflows


#### ✗ What we don’t like about Originality.ai


- Tendency to over-flag ambiguous or mixed content
- Less intuitive interface compared to teacher-focused tools
- Requires manual privacy opt-out for data sharing


### How Much Does Originality.ai Cost?


Pricing is flexible. You can pay $14.95/month for a subscription or go pay-as-you-go at $30 for 3,000 credits. That flexibility makes it easier to pitch to department heads who don’t want recurring costs without proven ROI.


Audit trails are the standout feature. When an academic integrity case escalates to administration, having a documented detection history with timestamps and confidence scores gives teachers credible evidence. No other detector I tested makes this workflow as seamless.


#### Originality.ai is suitable for:


- Teacher teams and departments that need shared dashboards and audit trails
- Department heads who want centralized billing and reporting
- Schools that need documentation for escalated integrity cases


#### Originality.ai is not suitable for:


- Individual teachers (GPTZero is a better fit)
- Educators who want a simple, teacher-friendly interface


**Bottom line:** Originality.ai beats GPTZero for team workflows but falls short for individual teachers. It’s available without institutional adoption, unlike Turnitin, making it the practical middle ground for department-level purchases.


## How to Choose the Right AI Detector for Your Classroom


To choose the right AI detector for your classroom, you should evaluate five key factors that directly impact students and teaching workflows. While this guide ranks the top options, your specific classroom context determines which tradeoffs matter most.


- **ESL false positive rate:** If you teach non-native English speakers, this is your first filter. GPTZero’s 38% ESL false positive rate means over a third of legitimate ESL student work gets wrongly flagged. Copyleaks at ~13% is the safest choice for multilingual classrooms.
- **Humanizer resilience:** Students are increasingly running AI text through paraphrasing tools. GPTZero drops to 18% detection on humanized content. Pangram is the only tool that claims to catch humanizer output. If evasion is your concern, this is the deciding factor.
- **FERPA/COPPA compliance:** Not automatic with any tool. Schools must request Data Processing Agreements from vendors. Pangram holds SOC 2 Type 2 certification. Updated COPPA rules take effect in April 2026 with stricter requirements for tools collecting data from minors.
- **Cost-per-student:** AI Writing Check is free. GPTZero’s free tier covers 10,000 words/month. Turnitin runs $2.59-3.19/student/year with institutional contracts. Evaluate whether the detection gaps in free tools matter for your specific needs before committing budget.
- **LMS integration:** Turnitin and Copyleaks integrate with most major platforms. Winston AI connects to Google Classroom. Pangram covers Canvas, Moodle, Google Classroom, and Schoology. Copy-paste workflows don’t scale for teachers grading 30+ essays.

### How to Choose the Right AI Detector for Your Classroom


**ESL false positive rate:** If you teach non-native English speakers, this is your first filter. GPTZero’s 38% ESL false positive rate means over a third of legitimate ESL student work gets wrongly flagged. Copyleaks at ~13% is the safest paid option for multilingual classrooms, and Pangram recorded zero false positives on the TOEFL essay set from the Stanford study. Avoid QuillBot here, since its ~13% figure is a general rate with no ESL-specific testing behind it.


**Humanizer resilience:** Students are increasingly running AI text through paraphrasing tools. GPTZero drops to 18% detection on humanized content and QuillBot falls to roughly 60% on hybrid human-AI writing. Pangram is the only tool that holds up on paraphrased output. If evasion is your concern, this is the deciding factor.


**Process visibility:** A detection score tells you what a document looks like. It cannot tell you how it was written. Grammarly Authorship fills that gap for free by tracking typed, pasted, AI-generated, and AI-edited text as the student works, and replaying the session on demand. Pair it with a scoring tool rather than choosing between them.


**FERPA/COPPA compliance:** Not automatic with any tool. Schools must request Data Processing Agreements from vendors. Pangram holds SOC 2 Type 2 certification and GPTZero holds SOC 2. Grammarly for Education offers institutional DPAs, and free consumer tools like QuillBot require you to check terms before putting student work through them. Updated COPPA rules take effect in April 2026 with stricter requirements for tools collecting data from minors.


**Cost-per-student:** Grammarly Authorship and QuillBot are free. GPTZero’s free tier covers 10,000 words per month. Pangram starts at $20 per month for 300,000 words. Turnitin runs $2.59 to $3.19 per student per year with institutional contracts. Evaluate whether the detection gaps in free tools matter for your specific needs before committing budget.


**LMS integration:** Turnitin and Copyleaks integrate with most major platforms. Pangram covers Canvas, Moodle, Google Classroom, and Schoology. Grammarly reaches Canvas, Blackboard, and Moodle plus Google Docs and Word. Winston AI connects to Google Classroom. QuillBot has no LMS integration at all. Copy-paste workflows do not scale for teachers grading 30+ essays.


## Final Verdict: Which AI Detector Do I Recommend for Teachers?


Pangram wins for accuracy and humanizer detection, with the lowest false positive rate of any tool tested. For teachers with zero budget, GPTZero’s free tier of 10,000 words per month is the strongest starting point. For ESL and multilingual classrooms, Copyleaks’ ~13% false positive rate makes it the safest choice.


If your school already pays for Turnitin, use it, but pair it with a second detector for Claude-generated content and ESL students. For teacher teams, Originality.ai’s shared dashboards and audit trails fill a workflow gap. For schools with zero budget and zero tech infrastructure, AI Writing Check from Quill.org costs nothing and includes a teacher toolkit.


## FAQ


### What should I do when an AI detector flags student work?


Start with a private conversation, not an accusation. The Cornell framework recommends comparing flagged work against in-class writing samples, reviewing revision history, and asking the student to explain their process verbally. John Grady’s research found that combining detector output with revision history raises accuracy to about 75%. Grammarly Authorship and Google Docs version history both give you that revision record for free. A verbal defense method, where the student walks you through their argument and sources, often reveals more than any algorithm. Never confront a student publicly or treat a detection score as a verdict on its own.


### Are AI detectors biased against ESL students?


Yes, significantly. Stanford found that 61.22% of TOEFL essays by non-native speakers were wrongly flagged as AI-generated. Chinese students faced a 61.3% false positive rate versus 5.1% for US students. Pangram recorded zero false positives when evaluated against the same 91 TOEFL essays from that study, and Copyleaks performs best among the mainstream detectors at roughly 13%. GPTZero sits at 38%, which makes it the riskiest choice for a multilingual classroom. If you teach non-native speakers, ESL accuracy should be your first filter when choosing a tool. The consequences of a false accusation fall hardest on students already navigating language barriers.


### Can students beat AI detectors?


Yes, and many already do. Humanizer tools reduce detection from nearly 100% to around 18%. In testing, Turnitin’s accuracy dropped from 92% to 0% with advanced paraphrasing. There are now 150+ humanizer tools drawing 33.9 million monthly visits, and the most popular paraphraser, QuillBot, is widely used by students for exactly this. Pangram is the one tool that holds up on paraphrased output, though independent verification is still limited. Assume motivated students will find workarounds, and lean on process evidence like Grammarly Authorship or Google Docs version history rather than the score alone.


### Are AI detection tools FERPA and COPPA compliant?


Not automatically. Schools must request Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) from vendors and verify compliance independently. Updated COPPA rules take effect in April 2026 with stricter requirements for any tools collecting data from minors. Pangram holds SOC 2 Type 2 certification and claims FERPA compliance. GPTZero has SOC 2 certification. Grammarly for Education offers institutional DPAs and admin controls, though the free consumer version is licensed to the individual student rather than the school. Free tools with no education tier, including QuillBot, should be checked against your district’s policy before student work goes through them. Always verify directly with the vendor and your district’s legal or compliance team before deploying any detection tool at scale.


### How much do AI detectors cost per student?


Grammarly Authorship is free on every tier and QuillBot is free with no signup. GPTZero works out to roughly $1.27 per student at scale, based on Shaker Heights’ $5,600 per year for 4,400 students. Pangram starts at $20 per month for 300,000 words, with a $65 tier covering 1.5 million. Copyleaks runs $10.99 per month for individuals. Turnitin is the most expensive at $2.59 to $3.19 per student per year and requires institutional purchasing. Start with free tools to evaluate fit, then upgrade only if the detection gaps matter for your specific classroom needs.


### Can an AI detector score be used as proof of cheating?


No. Every vendor explicitly warns against using detection scores as standalone evidence of academic dishonesty, including QuillBot, which tells users on its own product page never to rely on AI detection alone for decisions affecting someone’s academic standing. Courts have upheld students’ 14th Amendment due process rights in misconduct cases (Goss v. Lopez). Multiple lawsuits are currently pending against universities that relied solely on detector scores to discipline students. Treat scores as one data point in a broader investigation, never as a verdict.


### Should I redesign assignments instead of using detectors?


Both. Detectors flag potential issues, but redesigned assignments reduce the incentive to use AI in the first place. Effective strategies include staged drafts with required checkpoints, personal reflection topics tied to individual experiences, shared Google Docs where you can view revision history in real time, requiring a Grammarly Authorship report alongside the submission, and oral defense components where students explain their reasoning. The goal is learning, not surveillance. Use detectors to identify where support is needed, then redesign to make the work harder to outsource.
